channel.title: Hendro Kuswantoro
channel.description: Notes on maps, spatial data and the systems around them.

item.title: When a map should say I do not know
item.dc:creator: Hendro Kuswantoro
item.description: My parking map does not answer outside Yogyakarta. Here is why.
item.content:encoded:
My parking map covers Yogyakarta city only. Outside it there is no zone and no fee. That is on purpose.

The rule only lives in one city

The fee follows a Yogyakarta city rule. That rule does not apply in Purworejo, in Bandung, or out at sea. A map that still shows a number there is making up a rule.

The first version did that. Every point far from a zoned street became Zone III, one thousand rupiah, anywhere in the world. It looked tidy. It was wrong.

What the app does now

Now the app carries a boundary, drawn from the roads it really has. Inside it you get a zone and a fee. Outside it both stay empty, and the screen says the point is out of range.

Zero is a reading. Missing data is not. The two must never look the same.

Why bother

Saying nothing feels weak. But a wrong number gets copied, argued over, and printed. It lives much longer than a moment of disappointment.

People notice which app admits it does not know. That is the app they believe when it answers.

item.title: A hotspot is not a fire
item.dc:creator: Hendro Kuswantoro
item.description: A satellite sees heat, not flames. Small difference, big effect.
item.content:encoded:
Every dry season the hotspot maps come around. One red dot is read as one fire. But a satellite sees heat, not flames.

What the satellite sees

The sensor compares one patch of ground with the ground around it. If the patch is much hotter, it gets flagged. The patch is about 375 metres across. So one dot is a hot patch of land, not one flame.

Heat is not always a land fire. A factory chimney, a furnace, a brick kiln, even a metal roof at noon can be flagged.

No dots does not mean safe

This side is missed more often. The satellite passes a few times a day and clouds block the view. A fire under thick cloud never shows up.

A hotspot map answers one question. Where the satellite saw heat, at the hour it passed.

How I use them

I group the dots first. Dots close in place and time become one event, with a start, a direction and an end.

Then every map says which sensor, which date and hour, and how sure the reading is. A reader can judge it, not just trust the red.

item.title: Why the source always goes in the corner
item.dc:creator: Hendro Kuswantoro
item.description: The small text in the corner decides if a map can be trusted. It holds three things.
item.content:encoded:
A map is often judged by its colours. What decides if it can be used is the small text in the corner.

Three things that must be there

Where the data came from, named by agency or by file, not the word internet. When it was taken, because land cover last year and this year can differ a lot. The coordinate system and the scale, so people know if distances may be measured.

If there is room I add one more, who made the map and when. So there is someone to ask when something looks odd.

A map with no source note is not a map. It is a picture shaped like an island.

Why it matters

A printed map lives long. It goes on a wall, gets photographed, gets sent to a group, then used a year later by someone who was not in the meeting. All they have is that corner.

So I write that part first, before the colours. If the source is not clear, the map is not ready.
